summary: Discusses common reasons protocol implementations run slowly and how to organize them into modules without hurting efficiency. It is advice for implementers rather than a protocol.

eli5.summary: A program that follows too many neat steps can become slow. This memo explains how to build network software that is tidy and still quick.

questions: should tcp run in the kernel
how to speed up tcp checksum
subtitle: Clark's 1982 case that neat layering costs speed, and how to structure a protocol implementation to get both.

tldr.problem: Protocol implementers often find their code runs slower than hoped, and the blame lands on protocol design or the operating system.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC argues that how an implementation is modularized and fitted into the operating system matters most, compares the process, kernel and front-end options, and lists tuning rules such as optimizing the expected case and avoiding data copies.
tldr.outcome: It concludes that layering is a mixed blessing, that performance rarely comes from one fix, and that it is hard to retrofit. It is Informational advice, not a protocol.

today: RFC 817 is an Informational memo from July 1982 and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It is implementation advice from its era and defines no protocol.

sections.title: What Efficiency Means
sections.content:
The RFC names three goals that often conflict: sending data at minimum transmission cost, sending at a high rate, and using as few computer resources as possible. So there may be no such thing as a successful general purpose protocol implementation.

It works an example. With 576-byte packets, the maximum generally acceptable internet packet size, and 4288 bits of useful data per packet, a throughput of 10,000 bits per second needs a packet about every 430 milliseconds. At 100 kilobits per second the gap is 43 milliseconds, and at one megabit per second no more than 4.3 milliseconds. Interrupt service, process scheduling, disk fetches of 30 to 100 milliseconds and scheduling quanta of 100 milliseconds or more can eat that time. Per-packet cost is dominated by factors independent of packet size, so two rules follow: send data in large packets, and never send an unneeded packet. RFC 813 covers one way to send fewer packets.
sections.eli5: Mailing a letter costs about the same whether it holds one word or a whole page, so write fuller letters, and never mail an empty envelope.

sections.title: Where the Protocol Lives
sections.content:
There are three usual places to put a protocol: in a process, in the operating system kernel, or in a separate communications processor (front end). A process is easy for someone who is not a kernel expert, but suffers scheduling delay and may be unable to provide services normally reached through kernel entry points. Server telnet is the worst case, since local terminal handlers live in the kernel.

The kernel avoids those problems but has its own. Protocols need complex actions on timeouts, and the kernel often has no process to run them, leaving interrupt time, where actions can mask interrupts too long, the environment is primitive, the scheduler cannot be invoked, and a flood of packets can use all the time. Kernel address space may also be too small, and the code may need rework with every operating system change. A front end can be tailored and reused across hosts, but costs an extra computer and the host still needs code, itself protocol-like, to talk to it. The RFC also describes the last-resort trick of wiring a front end to teletype ports, which Michael Padlipsky called the "milking machine" approach and which is very inflexible.
sections.eli5: You can have the helper work in your room, in the busy front office, or in a separate building. Each place is handy in one way and annoying in another.

sections.title: Layering and Where to Slice
sections.content:
The real question is how to slice the whole protocol family between the kernel and user processes. Slicing at the top of TCP makes the TCP interface mimic other devices, since TCP gives a bidirectional byte stream, but puts TCP in the kernel. Slicing above Telnet adds so much kernel code that in some early implementations the network package rivals the size of the rest of the supervisor.

Moving all of TCP out of the kernel is awkward because TCP, like IP, demultiplexes incoming data, so a separate TCP process would be scheduled before the user process. The alternative is to slice along a functional boundary: keep just enough IP and TCP in the kernel to know which process a datagram is for, then route it there for the rest of the processing. This removes timer-based actions from the kernel and shrinks it, and RFC 814 discusses it further. It also means one TCP per connection, so one could be tuned for file transfer and another for Telnet. The RFC notes this approach is by no means generally accepted but deserves consideration.
sections.eli5: Instead of one mailroom sorting everything, the building only checks which apartment a letter is for and hands it over. Each apartment then opens and handles its own mail.

sections.title: Layer Barriers and Packet Sharing
sections.content:
Independent layers decide independently when to send packets. With server telnet echoing characters, one arriving packet makes TCP owe an acknowledgement, Telnet or the application owe an echo, and possibly Telnet control actions, so several packets go back. Combining them reduces common carrier charges and scheduling work in both hosts.

The remedy is to let a limited amount of information leak across layer barriers. For example, TCP could ask the layer above whether to pause a few milliseconds before acknowledging, hoping to piggyback on outgoing data. That helps with server Telnet but is unacceptable for file transfer, where data rarely flows the other way and delay holds up the next packets. The RFC compares a firm layer boundary to a file system: it helps naive users, but database builders go around it and trade modularity for efficiency. It says the dilemma will ease only when programmers are willing to weave some protocol structure into their applications.
sections.eli5: If three helpers each send you a separate note about one event, you get three envelopes. If they talk first, they can send one envelope, but they must know a bit about each other's jobs.

sections.title: Tuning IP and TCP Processing
sections.content:
IP is simple apart from fragmentation and reassembly (see RFC 815). Most IP cost is table look-up: internet address to gateway, then gateway to local network. With as many as a thousand network numbers, a linear search on every packet is unsuitable, and TCP may cache a hint per connection to pass to IP.

In TCP the checksum is the well-known overhead, but it is central and no implementor should omit validating it. The RFC suggests a checksum instruction, combining it with a copy, and careful coding. On Multics, an early version needed 6 milliseconds for a 576-byte segment and a recoded one took under one millisecond. Another rule is to optimize the expected case: assume the next packet is the next one in sequence, check that only ACK, and possibly Push, are set, and keep the resequencing list searched from highest sequence number down. Keep the retransmission queue tuned for discarding, perhaps rebuilding packets only when needed. Finally, avoid copying data: in the Multics example, about three milliseconds per 576-byte packet split into one millisecond of checksum, 600 microseconds of copying, and .7 milliseconds for header processing and resequencing.
sections.eli5: Plan for the usual case: most mail arrives in order and is plain. Do not carry the same box from room to room if you can leave it in place.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
Time usually goes equally to all parts of a program, so with the possible exception of checksumming, few people find one single bottleneck. Performance comes from painstaking tuning of the whole program. Depending on traffic, either structure or packet handling can dominate, for example one-byte Telnet packets versus maximum-size file transfer packets.

The RFC calls layering a mixed blessing. A layer interface is needed when several clients share a layer, but a fixed interface leaves layers poorly informed about each other's needs, and a boundary that comes from the specification need not be the right boundary for the implementation. Good performance is hard to retrofit and may require redoing the program from the bottom up, so designers should think about correctness and performance together from the start.
sections.eli5: Speed usually comes from many small improvements, not one big trick, and it is much easier to plan for it from the start than to fix it later.

viz.caption: THREE PLACES TO PUT A PROTOCOL (RFC 817)

items.title: In a process
items.text: Easy to build, but scheduling delay and hard to match kernel interfaces.

items.title: In the kernel
items.text: Fits devices, but timeouts, interrupt time and space are problems.

items.title: In a front end
items.text: Tailored and reusable, but costs a machine and still needs host code.
